meta.name: Bluetick Coonhound Grooming Guide
meta.excerpt: Bluetick Coonhound coat maintenance is minimal. Ear care is not — the long pendant ears require weekly attention to prevent the chronic infections that are the breed's primary health management task.
meta.meta_description: Bluetick Coonhound grooming guide: short ticked coat care, critical ear cleaning protocol, post-swimming ear care, nail and dental maintenance.

intro.label: The Bluetick's Coat
intro.heading: A Coat That's Easy — Ears That Aren't
intro.html:
Run a hand down a Bluetick Coonhound and you'll feel why owners call this a wash-and-wear breed: short, dense, glossy hair lying flat against the body, with almost no undercoat to speak of. The famous blue-black ticking scattered over a white base isn't painted on with grooming — it's baked into the hair itself, and a clean, well-fed Bluetick shows that mottled pattern with barely any brushing at all. This is a single-layer coat built for a working scenthound that spends hours moving through brush and water, not a coat designed to be styled or shaped. That's good news for anyone weighing the time commitment of a 45–80 lb hound: the body coat itself is close to the lowest-maintenance category on the breed spectrum.

A weekly pass with a rubber curry mitt or a hound glove is genuinely sufficient. The rubber nubs lift dead hair and distribute natural skin oils across the coat, which is what keeps the ticking looking rich rather than dull. Shedding is steady and moderate year-round rather than explosive — Blueticks don't carry a wool-like undercoat that blows out in dramatic clumps twice a year the way a spitz breed's does. You'll find hair on the couch every week, just never in the fistfuls a double-coated dog produces during a seasonal coat change.

Puppy Coat to Adult Coat

Bluetick puppies are born with a softer, slightly fuzzier version of the adult coat, and the ticking pattern itself is often not fully set until somewhere between 4 and 8 months — a pup that looks mostly white at birth will darken in visibly as the mottling develops. Grooming needs during this stage are minimal but the socialization work matters more: get a young Bluetick used to having ears lifted, paws handled, and a brush run over the body before the adult coat and the adult ear-canal maintenance routine are both in full swing. By around 12–18 months the coat has reached its mature density and texture, and the weekly mitt routine described above becomes the permanent adult schedule.

The Shedding Calendar

Because there's no heavy undercoat to shed seasonally, a Bluetick's shedding calendar is fairly flat across the year, with only mild upticks. Late spring tends to bring a slightly heavier week or two of loose hair as the coat lightens for summer, and dogs kept mostly outdoors or in variable climates may show a similarly mild increase in early fall. Neither event requires daily brushing the way a genuine coat-blow does in double-coated breeds — bumping the weekly mitt session to twice a week for those few weeks is plenty.

Why the Ears Are the Real Job

The coat is the easy part. The long, heavy, pendant ears that hang well past the muzzle are the actual grooming priority for this breed, and they deserve more attention than the body coat gets. Those ears were bred to help funnel ground scent up toward the nose while trailing, but the same shape that makes a Bluetick an excellent cold-nose tracker also seals off airflow to the ear canal. Warm, low-oxygen, low-light conditions inside a hanging ear are exactly what yeast and bacteria need to establish an infection, and a Bluetick that swims, works in wet brush, or lives somewhere humid is at meaningfully higher risk than a prick-eared breed of similar size. Treat ear maintenance as a non-negotiable weekly task, not an occasional one.

Tools for the Job

  • Rubber grooming mitt or hound glove — the core weekly tool for the body coat
  • Vet-approved ear cleaning solution formulated for dogs, not water or rubbing alcohol
  • Soft cotton balls or gauze squares (avoid cotton swabs inside the canal)
  • Dog-specific shampoo — a deodorizing formula is worth having on hand for hound odor between baths
  • Heavy-duty nail clippers or a grinder sized for a large dog's nails
  • A soft-bristle or rubber-bristle dental brush and enzymatic dog toothpaste

care.label: Ear Care Protocol
care.heading: The Weekly Ear Routine That Prevents Most Infections
care.html:
If there is one grooming habit that matters more than any other for a Bluetick Coonhound, it's a consistent weekly ear check. Pick a day — bath night, or the same evening you do the coat mitt-down — and make the ear check part of that routine rather than something you remember only after an infection has already started. Dogs that are handled this way from puppyhood tend to tolerate the process without a fight, which matters given how large and heavy an adult Bluetick's ears are compared to a smaller breed's.

Step by Step

  1. Lift the ear flap fully away from the head and look at the visible canal opening and the inner surface of the flap itself.
  2. A healthy ear is pale pink inside, has only a small amount of light tan or clear wax, and has no noticeable smell.
  3. Warning signs include redness or inflammation, dark brown or black discharge, a yeasty or sour odor, head shaking, scratching at the ear, or visible swelling.
  4. If everything looks and smells normal, a dry cotton ball wiped gently around the visible folds is all that's needed — you're done for the week.
  5. If there's mild wax buildup, dampen a cotton ball with a vet-formulated cleaner and wipe the visible canal and the inner flap surface. Let the dog shake its head afterward to help clear residual fluid rather than trying to dry the canal manually with a swab.
  6. If you see redness, dark discharge, or catch that sour smell, don't just clean it and hope — a Bluetick's L-shaped ear canal traps infection deep enough that home cleaning alone rarely resolves an active case. Get a vet appointment and expect a prescription ear medication.

Signs at a Glance

Healthy EarNeeds a Vet
Pale pink canalRed, inflamed canal
Little to no odorYeasty or sour smell
Light, clear waxDark brown or black discharge
No head shakingFrequent shaking, scratching, whining when touched

After Water or Bath Time

Because Blueticks were developed to work through creeks and swamps chasing cold trails, plenty of them love water — and every swim is an opportunity for moisture to get trapped under that heavy ear flap. Dry the ears deliberately after any water exposure: tilt the head to each side and gently towel-dry the outer ear and as much of the visible canal as you can reach. A dog that swims regularly or lives near a pond needs this after every single swim, not just on the weekly schedule. Skipping this step is the single most common reason a Bluetick that was doing fine suddenly develops a smelly, red ear in July.

What Makes Bluetick Ears Different

Compared to a shorter-eared hound or a prick-eared working breed, the sheer size and weight of a Bluetick's ear leather means less air circulates underneath it even when the dog is standing still or lying down. Some owners find it helps to occasionally flip the ears back (not pinned, just briefly exposed) during warm, humid weather to let air reach the canal opening, though this is a supplement to the cleaning routine, not a replacement for it. If you notice your dog tilting its head persistently to one side, or if it seems reluctant to have that ear touched at all, treat it as a same-week vet visit rather than something to monitor for a few more days — established infections in this breed's ear shape tend to need prescription treatment rather than resolving with home cleaning alone.

special.label: Coat, Nails, Teeth, and the Full Routine
special.heading: Rounding Out the Grooming Routine
special.html:
Coat and bathing: Between weekly mitt sessions, plan on a full bath every 6–8 weeks, or sooner if the natural hound scent becomes noticeable to you or guests. That scent is a normal feature of the breed's oil-rich short coat, not a hygiene failure, and a deodorizing dog shampoo handles it well without needing to bathe more often than that. Use lukewarm water, work the shampoo in against the direction of hair growth to lift debris from the dense coat, then rinse thoroughly — leftover shampoo residue is a common cause of itchy skin in short-coated dogs. Because a Bluetick's coat has almost no undercoat to trap water, drying is fast: a towel-dry followed by 10–15 minutes of air-drying (or a low, cool-setting dryer if the dog tolerates it) is usually enough, which is a real advantage over longer or double-coated breeds that can take an hour to dry through.

Nails

Trim monthly, or whenever you hear clicking on hard floors — a large hound's nails grow fast enough that this schedule genuinely needs to be a calendar habit, not an occasional afterthought. Heavy-duty clippers or a grinder built for larger nails are worth the investment; standard small-dog clippers struggle with the thickness of an adult Bluetick's nail. Start handling paws and doing brief practice trims from puppyhood, since a dog this size that dislikes nail trims can become a genuine two-person job later on.

Teeth

Brush 2–3 times a week with an enzymatic dog toothpaste, starting at the front teeth (the easiest for both of you to tolerate) and gradually working back toward the molars as the dog gets comfortable. Consistent home brushing is the cheapest and most effective thing an owner can do to reduce the frequency and cost of professional dental cleanings down the road, and it matters for every breed regardless of coat type.

DIY vs. Professional Grooming for a Bluetick

Most Bluetick owners never need a professional groomer for the coat itself — a short, single-layer coat this manageable rarely justifies the expense. Where a groomer earns their fee is bath logistics: a 45–80 lb dog in a home tub is a real undertaking, and a shop with a raised, large-capacity tub and a proper drain can turn a wrestling match into a 20-minute job. A realistic professional schedule looks like this:

ServiceCostFrequency
Bath, blow-dry, brush-out, nail trim$40–$70Every 6–10 weeks, optional
Add-on ear cleaning$10–$20Same visit
Nail trim/grind only$15–$25Monthly, if you'd rather outsource it

If you do bring your Bluetick to a groomer, tell them explicitly about the ear care protocol and ask them to check and clean as part of the visit — a groomer unfamiliar with heavy-eared scenthounds may skip a thorough ear check unless asked. Anyone doing this at home instead can build a starter kit — mitt, clippers or grinder, ear cleaner, dental brush and paste, deodorizing shampoo — for roughly $60–$100, and that kit lasts well over a year for a single dog.

Grooming Mistakes That Trip Up Bluetick Owners Specifically

  • Treating the ears as optional because the coat is so easy. Owners who fall into a false sense of low-maintenance security based on the short coat are the ones who end up with recurring ear infections. The coat and the ears are two separate jobs with two separate schedules.
  • Skipping the post-swim dry-off. A quick towel around the body and nothing done to the ears leaves moisture trapped exactly where it does the most damage in this breed.
  • Reaching for a de-shedding rake anyway. Because the coat is short and single-layered, an undercoat rake or de-shedding blade has almost nothing to grab and can irritate the skin without actually reducing shedding — a rubber mitt does the job better and more gently on this coat type.
  • Ignoring hound odor until it's strong. A mild oily-coat smell is normal between baths; letting it build for months before bathing usually means the coat has also picked up enough surface grime to irritate the skin.
  • Under-drying after a bath and assuming the short coat handles itself. It usually does dry fast, but skin folds around the neck and the base of the ears can stay damp longer than the rest of the coat and are worth a deliberate towel pass.

Paws and Skin, Weekly

While you're doing the weekly ear check and mitt pass, run hands over the paws and skin too. Working scenthounds that spend time in brush and fields pick up grass awns between the toes, and a large hound's paw pads take real wear during the 60–90 minutes of daily exercise this breed genuinely needs. A quick weekly look for cracked pads, ticks, hot spots, or anything unusual on the skin turns grooming time into a low-cost early warning system rather than a purely cosmetic task.

faq.q: How often do Blueticks get ear infections, and can it be prevented?
faq.a: Without a consistent routine, fairly often — the heavy pendant ear and any regular swimming both work against airflow to the canal. Owners who commit to a weekly lift-and-check, plus a deliberate dry-off after every swim or bath, can often go months or years between infections. It's rarely a one-time fix; think of it as an ongoing habit tied to the dog's lifestyle, not a problem you solve once and forget.

faq.q: Do Bluetick Coonhounds need a professional groomer?
faq.a: Not for the coat itself — a short single-layer coat this easy rarely justifies the expense. Some owners do use a groomer purely for bath logistics, since managing a wet 45–80 lb dog in a home tub is genuinely harder than it sounds. If you do book a groomer, specifically ask them to check and clean the ears, since a shop unused to heavy-eared scenthounds may not think to look.

faq.q: Why does my Bluetick smell like a 'hound dog' even after a bath?
faq.a: Some level of oily-coat scent is a normal feature of this breed's short, dense hair, not a sign anything is wrong. It tends to build gradually between baths as skin oils accumulate on the coat. A deodorizing dog shampoo every 6–8 weeks manages it well; bathing much more often than that isn't necessary and can actually dry out the skin, making the smell worse rather than better.

faq.q: Is shedding a big issue with this breed?
faq.a: No — this is one of the easier hound coats to live with day to day. There's minimal undercoat, so you won't see the dramatic seasonal coat-blows that double-coated breeds go through. Expect a steady, moderate amount of loose hair year-round with a mild uptick for a couple of weeks in spring, manageable with one extra brushing session during that stretch.

faq.q: What's the single most important grooming habit for a Bluetick owner?
faq.a: The weekly ear check, without question. The coat genuinely takes care of itself with a once-a-week mitt pass, but the long pendant ears are a standing risk factor for infection that only a consistent lift-and-look habit, plus post-swim drying, keeps under control. Owners who treat this as optional are the ones who end up managing chronic ear problems later.
